candidates.title: Alcohol and cardiovascular disease: inter-organ crosstalk, microvascular dysfunction, and cardiovascular ageing.
candidates.abstract: Alcohol-related cardiovascular risk is being fundamentally reappraised. Observational associations suggesting cardioprotection with light-to-moderate drinking have been challenged by contemporary cohort analyses, Mendelian-randomization studies, biomarker-informed investigations, and updated public-health guidance. Uncertainty nevertheless persists at very low exposure levels and for selected coronary or all-cause outcomes. Alcohol is therefore best viewed as a dose-, pattern-, and host-dependent cardiovascular stressor. Acute or binge drinking, sustained heavy intake, chronic intake with episodic binges, and withdrawal produce overlapping but distinct phenotypes, including hypertension, atrial fibrillation, ventricular arrhythmias, sudden death, alcohol-associated cardiomyopathy, heart failure, stroke, and vascular disease. A systems-cardiology framework is presented in which direct myocardial injury, electrical instability, haemodynamic and autonomic stress, vascular and microvascular dysfunction, and disrupted inter-organ signalling interact. Ethanol and acetaldehyde toxicity, redox imbalance, microbial and inflammatory mediators, neurohumoral activation, and metabolic or electrolyte disturbances can impair endothelial signalling, mitochondrial energetics, excitation-contraction coupling, electrical stability, and repair. Pathway dominance varies across exposure patterns and susceptible hosts; coronary microvascular dysfunction may represent a convergence pathway rather than an obligatory mediator. Cumulative injury can diminish perfusion, contractile, electrical, autonomic, and exercise reserve. Alcohol-related cardiovascular ageing is proposed as a unifying cumulative phenotype encompassing mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative and nitrative stress, inflammageing, senescence, impaired repair, circadian and epigenetic dysregulation, fibrosis, and ventriculo-arterial uncoupling, although direct human evidence remains incomplete. Age, biological sex, genetics, comorbidities, sleep-circadian disruption, nutrition, medications, and polysubstance misuse may modify pathway dominance and reversibility. Structured exposure assessment and alcohol reduction or abstinence, when indicated, are actionable components of cardiovascular prevention and care.

candidates.title: Safety and Efficacy of Transvenous Lead Extraction Using a Right-Sided Approach.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite extensive experience with transvenous lead extraction (TLE) overall, outcomes for systems implanted on the right chest remain underexplored, largely because of their low incidence.
OBJECTIVES: The objective was to evaluate whether system laterality influences TLE outcomes.
METHODS: Using our institutional, prospectively maintained ExTRACT registry, we analyzed all consecutive patients undergoing TLE procedures at the Cleveland Clinic between 1996 and 2022. Patients were categorized by system laterality. Baseline characteristics, procedural characteristics, and complications were assessed. Multivariable logistic regression models evaluated the association between right-sided TLE and adverse events.
RESULTS: Among 4,989 patients, 494 (9.9%) had right-sided and 4,495 (90.1%) had left-sided TLE. Compared with left-sided cases, right-sided cases had longer total lead dwell times (13.83 vs 9.26 years, P < 0.001) and were more likely to be extracted because of infection (47.57% vs 39.71%, P = 0.001). Fluoroscopy time was longer (15.95 vs 12.1 minutes; P < 0.001), and femoral workstation use more frequent (7.89% vs 4.05%, P < 0.001), yet complete extraction was lower (94.53% vs 96.44%, P = 0.034). Right-sided TLE had higher rates of sternotomy (2.83% vs 1.25%, P = 0.004) and superior vena cava or right atrial tear/perforation (2.49% vs 1.10%, P = 0.009). Thirty-day mortality was low and comparable (0.61% vs 0.47%, P = 0.727). Multivariable regression showed that right-sided TLE was associated with higher odds of sternotomy (OR = 1.92, 95% CI: 1.01-3.46, P = 0.037) and superior vena cava or right atrial tear/perforation (OR = 2.02, 95% CI: 1.01-3.78, P = 0.037).
CONCLUSIONS: Right-sided TLE is associated with a lower rate of complete extraction and increased procedural risk, particularly sternotomy and major vascular injury, compared with left-sided TLE. These findings should be carefully weighed when implanting or extracting right-sided systems.

candidates.title: Modified Posterior Wall Ablation in Persistent Atrial Fibrillation: the BOX-AF Randomized Clinical Trial.
candidates.abstract:
AIMS: The efficacy of left atrial posterior wall isolation (PWI) for persistent atrial fibrillation (AF) is controversial. We propose a modified left atrial posterior wall ablation strategy.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of modified posterior wall ablation in patients with persistent AF who underwent first-time radiofrequency catheter ablation.
METHODS AND RESULTS: In this multicenter, single-blind randomized trial, 276 patients with persistent AF were assigned 1:1 to pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) with (BOX+) or without modified posterior wall ablation (BOX-). Seven participants withdrew, leaving 269 (BOX+, n=139; BOX-, n=130) for primary endpoint analysis. The primary endpoint was freedom from any documented atrial arrhythmia lasting > 30 seconds without antiarrhythmic drugs after a 3 -month blanking period. At 12-month follow-up, the primary endpoint occurred in 120 of 139 patients (86.3%) in the BOX+ group and 113 of 130 (86.9%) in the BOX- group (hazard ratio 1.046, 95% CI, 0.54 - 2.01; P = 0.894). The BOX+ group exhibited longer procedure time and ablation time. Acute successful PWI was achieved in 91 (65.5%) patients assigned to BOX+. In a nonprespecified, post-randomization analysis, arrhythmia-free survival was 93.4% in patients with acute successful PWI, 72.9% in those with attempted but unsuccessful PWI, and 86.9% in controls without attempted PWI (overall log-rank P=0.002). Adverse events were similar between groups.
CONCLUSION: Routine addition of modified posterior wall ablation did not improve overall outcomes of first-time ablation in persistent AF. However, achieving successful PWI was associated with significantly lower recurrence.

candidates.title: Nonculprit Lesion Complexity and Timing of Complete Revascularization in Patients Presenting With Acute Coronary Syndrome and Multivessel Disease: Insights From the BIOVASC Trial.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The optimal timing of complete revascularization for patients with acute coronary syndrome, multivessel disease and complex nonculprit coronary lesions (NCL) remains unclear.
METHODS: The BIOVASC trial randomized patients with acute coronary syndrome and multivessel disease to immediate complete revascularization and staged complete revascularization. The primary end point was a composite of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, unplanned ischemia-driven revascularization, or cerebrovascular events at 2-year follow-up. In this exploratory post hoc analysis, patients were classified as having complex NCL if at least 1 nonculprit lesion met the following criteria: true bifurcation; severe calcification; lesion length >20 mm; aorto-ostial lesion; left main lesion. We aimed to compare a strategy of immediate complete revascularization and staged complete revascularization in patients presenting with acute coronary syndrome and multivessel disease with complex NCL. Moreover, we sought to compare patients with complex and noncomplex NCLs in terms of clinical outcomes.
RESULTS: Among the 1525 patients enrolled in the BIOVASC trial, 550 (36.1%) had a complex NCL. The presence of a complex NCL was associated with a significantly higher incidence of the primary end point compared with noncomplex NCL (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.49 [95% CI, 1.11-2.02]; P=0.01), including spontaneous myocardial infarction (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.86 [95% CI, 1.12-3.09]; P=0.02). In patients with complex NCL, the cumulative incidence of the primary end point was 15.7% in the immediate complete revascularization group and 17.5% in the staged complete revascularization group (hazard ratio, 0.86 [95% CI, 0.57-1.31]; P=0.49). No significant interaction was observed between the presence of a complex NCL and revascularization strategy for the primary end point (P for interaction=0.40).
CONCLUSIONS: In patients with acute coronary syndrome and multivessel disease, patients with complex NCL experienced worse clinical outcomes at 2-year follow-up, driven by higher rates of myocardial infarction. However, no statistically significant interaction was observed between NCL complexity and the effect of immediate complete revascularization versus staged complete revascularization.

candidates.title: Impact of Coronary Sinus Reducer on the Extent of Ischemia in Functional Stress Tests.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The coronary sinus reducer is an established therapy for patients with refractory angina due to obstructive coronary artery disease who are not candidates for further revascularization. Although symptomatic benefits are well documented, its effect on objective measures of ischemia remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the association between coronary sinus reducer implantation and inducible myocardial ischemia assessed by functional stress testing.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed a prospectively maintained registry of consecutive patients undergoing coronary sinus reducer implantation between 2011 and 2024. Baseline assessment included Canadian Cardiovascular Society angina class, 6-minute walk test, stress echocardiography, and dipyridamole single-photon emission computed tomography imaging, repeated at 6 months. Coprimary outcomes were changes in stress wall motion score index and in the proportion of patients with moderate or severe ischemia on single-photon emission computed tomography. Clinical nonresponders were defined as no improvement in Canadian Cardiovascular Society class at 12 months.
RESULTS: Among 153 treated patients, 118 had complete imaging data. Median stress wall motion score index improved from 1.38 to 1.23 (P<0.001), and stress left ventricular ejection fraction increased from 55% to 60% (P=0.019). The proportion of patients with moderate or severe ischemia on single-photon emission computed tomography decreased from 52% to 24% (P<0.001). The summed difference score, available in 45 patients, did not change significantly. Clinically, 86% improved by ≥1 Canadian Cardiovascular Society class at 6 months.
CONCLUSIONS: Coronary sinus reducer implantation was associated with reduced inducible ischemia on stress echocardiography and with clinical improvement. The proportion of patients with moderate or severe ischemia on single-photon emission computed tomography decreased following Reducer implantation.

candidates.title: Liver radiomics on routine cardiac CT identifies hepatic stress states that predict heart failure.
candidates.abstract:
AIMS: Heart failure (HF) prevention remains limited because early multisystem cardiometabolic dysfunction is not captured by conventional risk tools. We evaluated whether liver radiomic phenotypes derived opportunistically from coronary artery calcium computed tomography (CAC-CT) identify imaging-defined hepatic stress states associated with incident HF.
METHODS AND RESULTS: We analysed 59 237 individuals undergoing CAC-CT (CLARIFY: 46 028; Houston Methodist: 13 209). Liver regions were segmented and radiomic features extracted to derive a Liver Radiomics Score (LRS). The model was trained in a CLARIFY derivation cohort (Dtr, n = 9205), validated in a hold-out cohort (Dts, n = 36 823), and externally evaluated in Houston Methodist (Dext, n = 13 209). The mean follow-up was 1411 days (SD 760.1) in the pooled Dtr and Dts cohorts (1144 HF events) and 470 days (SD 596) in Dext (212 HF events). Continuous LRS was associated with incident HF [Dts: hazard ratio (HR) 1.63, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.52-1.74; P < 0.001; Dext: HR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.07; P = 0.004] and remained significant after multivariable adjustment in Dts. Increasing LRS quartiles showed progressively adverse hepatic, haemodynamic, and cardiometabolic profiles and higher HF risk. Among 17 806 Dts participants with PREVENT data, adding LRS modestly improved discrimination across CAC- and PREVENT-based models (P < 0.001) and improved reclassification metrics (7-year net reclassification improvement up to 0.25; including integrated discrimination improvement up to 0.015). High LRS identified elevated risk in low-risk groups: among participants with CAC=0, high LRS conferred ∼2.5-fold higher 5-year HF incidence, and ∼2.9-fold in PREVENT-low individuals.
CONCLUSION: In this large multicentre cohort, liver radiomics from CAC-CT captured hepatic stress states linked to HF risk and modestly improved risk stratification beyond CAC and PREVENT scores.

candidates.title: Effect of intensive blood pressure control on cognitive outcomes and brain structures in adults with type 2 diabetes: prespecified analysis of secondary outcomes of BPROAD randomised controlled trial.
candidates.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effect of intensive compared with standard treatment of systolic blood pressure (SBP) on cognitive outcomes and brain structures in adults with type 2 diabetes.
DESIGN: Multicentre, open label, outcome assessor masked, randomised controlled trial.
SETTING: 145 clinical centres across seven geographical regions in China.
PARTICIPANTS: 12 821 adults aged ≥50 years with type 2 diabetes, raised SBP, and increased cardiovascular risk, of whom 12 434 without probable dementia at baseline were included in this cognitive ancillary study. Further assessments were performed annually and at the end of study.
INTERVENTIONS: Participants were randomly assigned to receive intensive treatment targeting SBP <120 mm Hg or standard treatment targeting SBP <140 mm Hg for up to five years.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: The primary cognitive outcome was a composite of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment. Secondary cognitive outcomes included all cause dementia, mild cognitive impairment, changes in cognitive functions, and changes in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) characteristics. A subset of participants underwent brain MRI at baseline (n=862) and at the end of study (n=605) to assess changes in white matter lesion volume and total brain volume.
RESULTS: 6219 participants were assigned to receive intensive treatment and 6215 to receive standard treatment. Baseline mean age was 63.7 years, and 5567 (44.8%) participants were women. After one year, mean SBP was 121.6 mm Hg in the intensive treatment group and 133.2 mm Hg in the standard treatment group. During a median follow-up of 3.8 years, the primary cognitive outcome of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment occurred in 747 participants (3.69 events per 100 person years) in the intensive treatment group and 783 participants (3.89 events per 100 person years) in the standard treatment group (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.86 to 1.06; P=0.38). In the MRI substudy (428 intensive treatment v 434 standard treatment), the intensive treatment group had a smaller increase in white matter lesion volume compared with the standard treatment group (between group difference -0.09 inverse hyperbolic sine (asinh) transformed cm3, 95% CI -0.15 to -0.02; P=0.01).
CONCLUSIONS: Over a median of about four years, no statistically significant difference in incidence of a composite of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment was observed among adults with type 2 diabetes receiving standard treatment of SBP (target <140 mm Hg) and intensive treatment (target <120 mm Hg). Intensive treatment was, however, associated with a reduction in the accrual of cerebral white matter lesion volume.

candidates.title: Net Prolongation of Life with Ventricular Assist Device Support in Teenagers: Are We There Yet?
candidates.abstract: Heart transplantation prolongs survival in children with end-stage heart disease, yet a single donor heart does not provide a normal lifespan. Contemporary graft survival for teenagers is approximately 15 years, the shortest of any pediatric age group, and re-transplantation remains uncommon. For most patients, the first allograft is the only allograft. Recent adult data demonstrating survival with durable mechanical circulatory support comparable to transplantation raise an important question for adolescents: could intentionally extending ventricular assist device (VAD) support through the teenage years, with transplantation deferred to adulthood, increase total life-years? This perspective examines that hypothesis for adolescents with dilated cardiomyopathy. We review the heightened risks of rejection, graft loss, and treatment nonadherence during adolescence; contemporary outcomes with dischargeable durable VADs in children; the potential for myocardial recovery during extended support; and organ allocation policies that may unintentionally discourage a prolonged-support strategy. We also examine patient and family perspectives and discuss unresolved questions regarding stroke risk, allosensitization, long-term quality of life, and optimal timing of transplantation. No prospective data currently support intentional long-term VAD support as a bridge to transplantation in teenagers, and this concept should be viewed as a hypothesis rather than a practice recommendation. However, for carefully selected adolescents who are clinically stable on durable VAD support, delayed transplantation may be a reasonable topic for shared decision-making discussions while acknowledging the substantial uncertainties that remain. As durable device technology continues to improve, evaluating whether prolonged VAD support can achieve net prolongation of life in teenagers warrants prospective investigation.

candidates.title: Atrial fibrillation begets atrial fibrillation revisited: Early entrenchment of AF episodes.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The 7-day threshold defining persistent atrial fibrillation (AF) is clinically entrenched but biologically arbitrary. Whether episode termination follows scale-free dynamics or time-dependent entrenchment remains uncertain.
OBJECTIVE: To quantify the probability of spontaneous termination and assess its dependence on episode duration using large-scale pacemaker monitoring.
METHODS: Continuous pacemaker monitoring data from the ACaSA study were analyzed. Device-detected AF episodes were reconstructed from daily burden using predefined continuity rules. Termination was modelled as the conditional probability that an ongoing episode would terminate within the subsequent 24 hours. Duration dependence was assessed using a shared frailty Weibull survival model, and episode duration distributions were compared using the Vuong likelihood-ratio test.
RESULTS: After excluding patients with single-chamber devices or 100% baseline AF burden, 251 of 281 pacemaker recipients contributed 204,775 patient-days. Device-detected AF occurred in 154 patients, who contributed 7002 reconstructed episodes. Termination probability declined from 91.1% at 1 hour to 72.1% at 12 hours, 33.3% at 24 hours, and 4.3% at 7 days. Episode durations were better described by a lognormal distribution than by a scale-free power-law model.
CONCLUSION: Device-detected AF episodes show marked early entrenchment, with spontaneous termination becoming progressively less likely as episode duration increases. These findings support the concept that "AF begets AF" even at short timescales and suggest that persistence beyond 24 hours identifies a state with a substantially reduced likelihood of near-term spontaneous termination.

candidates.title: Treatment of Acute Ischemic Stroke: A Review.
candidates.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Acute ischemic stroke, caused by thrombotic or embolic occlusion of a cervical or cerebral artery, leads to neurologic injury due to sudden disruption of blood flow to the brain. Ischemic stroke is a leading cause of disability and death and accounts for about 85% of strokes in the US.
OBSERVATIONS: Symptoms of acute ischemic stroke vary based on the area of the affected brain. Common presentations include sudden arm or leg weakness, aphasia or slurred speech, sudden loss of balance or coordination, sudden visual difficulties, and/or facial drooping. Patients with suspected stroke should be transported to the nearest emergency department for urgent brain imaging, typically noncontrast computed tomography (CT). Based on 2026 American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (AHA/ASA) guidelines, first-line therapy for patients with acute ischemic stroke presenting within 4.5 hours from symptom onset with disabling symptoms (eg, affecting the ability to perform activities of daily living) is intravenous thrombolysis (tenecteplase or alteplase) in those without intracranial hemorrhage or other contraindications to thrombolysis. The treatment window can be extended to 9 hours-and up to 24 hours in patients with large vessel occlusion (eg, involving the internal carotid artery or proximal middle cerebral artery [M1 segment]) who are unable to receive thrombectomy-based on identification of salvageable tissue using perfusion imaging with CT perfusion or magnetic resonance imaging. In appropriately selected patients with acute ischemic stroke, pooled randomized trial data show an approximately 10% absolute increase in the probability of a better functional outcome with intravenous thrombolysis. Based on 2026 AHA/ASA guidelines, endovascular thrombectomy, which involves clot removal with an intra-arterial mechanical device, is recommended for patients with large vessel occlusion within 6 hours of stroke onset (class 1 recommendation) and is recommended in selected patients with large vessel occlusion within 24 hours of last known well (class 1 recommendation). Endovascular therapy should be performed after intravenous thrombolysis unless patients have contraindications to thrombolytic therapy. Compared with medical management, which includes intravenous thrombolysis when indicated, endovascular thrombectomy produces an approximately 20% absolute increase in functional independence.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Acute ischemic stroke causes substantial disability and mortality. First-line therapy for patients with disabling acute stroke symptoms is intravenous thrombolysis (if no contraindications) within 4.5 hours of stroke onset and up to 24 hours in carefully selected patients not receiving mechanical thrombectomy; for large vessel occlusions, mechanical thrombectomy may be performed up to 24 hours after stroke onset in eligible patients.

candidates.title: Long-Term Prognostic Value of Scar Characteristics in Cardiac Magnetic Resonance to Predict Appropriate Therapies in Primary Prevention.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) provides unique insights into ventricular arrhythmogenic substrate, although few studies have analyzed its long-term value in patients with implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) for primary prevention.
OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to evaluate the role of LGE characteristics in stratifying arrhythmogenic risk in patients with ICD implantation for primary prevention over long-term follow-up.
METHODS: This was a prospective study, between 2011 and 2017, in which 226 patients who underwent LGE CMR before ICD implantation for primary prevention were consecutively enrolled. Dedicated software (ADAS 3D) was used to quantify LGE, border zone, core, and conducting channels (CCs).
RESULTS: The median age was 62.9 years (Q1-Q3: 55.4-68.5 years), with 52% of participants (n = 104) with ischemic cardiomyopathy and a median MADIT (Multicenter Automatic Defibrillator Implantation Trial) score of 54 (Q1-Q3: 42-64). After a median follow-up period of 8.1 years (Q1-Q3: 6.2-10 years), 59 patients (29.5%) reached the primary endpoint (appropriate ICD therapy). LGE mass >10 g (HR: 3.58; 95% CI: 1.29-9.93; P = 0.014), CCs (HR: 3.42; 95% CI: 1.69-6.96; P = 0.009), and the presence of both LGE mass >10 g and CCs (34.92% vs 5.55%; HR: 4.65; 95% CI: 1.46-14.8; P = 0.009) were strongly associated with the primary endpoint. Patients without CCs and with LGE mass < 10 g had a very low rate of appropriate therapies (negative predictive value = 92%). LGE parameters remained independently associated with the primary endpoint after adjustment for MADIT score.
CONCLUSIONS: The characteristics of potential arrhythmia substrate assessed using LGE CMR are potent predictors of ventricular arrhythmias after ICD implantation for the primary prevention of sudden death.

candidates.title: Association of Left Ventricular Epicardial Adipose Tissue and Lipomatous Metaplasia With Ventricular Tachycardia Circuitry and Recurrence Following Ablation in Patients With Non-Ischemic Cardiomyopathy.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients with nonischemic cardiomyopathy (NICM) have complex intramural ventricular tachycardia (VT) circuitry and relatively high postablation recurrences.
OBJECTIVES: This study evaluated the association of left ventricular epicardial adipose tissue (LV EAT) and lipomatous metaplasia (LM) with critical VT circuitry and postablation VT recurrence in patients with NICM.
METHODS: In this retrospective study, we quantified LV EAT and LM via cardiac contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) in a cohort of consecutive patients with NICM before VT ablation. CECT image registration with VT critical sites in electroanatomic mapping was performed in a subset. Mixed-effects and subdistribution proportional hazard models were used to examine the association of image features with VT circuitry elements and outcomes, respectively.
RESULTS: In 48 patients with coregistered CECT-electroanatomic mapping, segmental maximal EAT thickness was associated with critical VT sites (OR: 1.36 per mm increase; P < 0.001), and a threshold of >4.7 mm EAT achieved 72% sensitivity and 71% specificity (OR: 2.15; P = 0.006) for VT site identification. This association remained significant after adjusting for LM, with a significant EAT-LM interaction (P = 0.027). Among all 119 patients, 52 experienced VT recurrence during a median follow-up of 1.7 years (Q1-Q3: 0.7-4.0). Lower LV EAT attenuation was independently associated with time to VT recurrence (subdistribution HR: 1.04 per 1 HU decrease; P = 0.012) after multivariable adjustment including LM and a significant LM interaction (P = 0.020).
CONCLUSIONS: LV EAT density and thickness are associated with VT circuitry and postablation recurrence in patients with NICM, and demonstrate a significant statistical interaction with LM.

candidates.title: Treatment of pulmonary hypertension in infants, children and young adults. 2026 consensus statement from the European Pediatric Pulmonary Vascular Disease Network (EPPVDN), endorsed by AHA, AEPC, EACTS, ESPR, PASCAR, PCS, and PICS.
candidates.abstract: The European Pediatric Pulmonary Vascular Disease Network (EPPVDN) is a registered, non-profit organization dedicated to advancing innovative diagnostic methods and treatment options for all forms of pediatric pulmonary vascular disease, including pulmonary hypertension (PH) related to congenital heart disease (CHD), PH associated with developmental lung disease (DEVLD-PH), persistent PH of the newborn (PPHN), postcapillary PH in left heart disease (PH-LHD), and associated cardiac dysfunction/heart failure. In the past, the EPPVDN has published consensus statements on the diagnosis and treatment of pediatric PH (2016, 2019), which have been endorsed by multiple societies. The executive writing group conducted comprehensive searches of the PubMed/MEDLINE bibliographic database (2000 to 2025) and engaged in multiple web-based and in-person meetings. Thirteen section task forces discussed and created consented recommendations. Prospective clinical studies, clinical trials, meta-analyses, expert consensus guidelines, and other articles with pediatric data were included in the search, using the terms 'pulmonary hypertension' and related keywords. Classes of recommendation (COR) and levels of evidence (LOE) were assigned based on AHA/ESC definitions, pediatric PH studies, adult studies including a minimum N number of 15 children, or studies involving adults with CHD. Classifications and definitions from the 7th World Symposium on Pulmonary Hypertension (WSPH) in 2024 were incorporated and discussed. We produced 6 graded recommendation tables (COR, LOE) and 3 algorithms for the treatment of pulmonary hypertension in infants, children, and young adults. A total of 16 main and 17 supplemental display items cover a range of topics, including risk assessment, pharmacological therapy, transcatheter interventions and surgery, recommendations specific to PH subgroups/special populations and clinical settings. Adaptation of management recommendations for middle-to-low-income regions is provided. Together, these up-to-date guidelines provide a comprehensive, detailed, and practical framework for the treatment of pulmonary hypertension in infants, children and young adults, aiming to improve outcomes and quality of life for affected patients.

candidates.title: Left Atrial Appendage Closure in Patients Considered Unsuitable for Oral Anticoagulation: Randomized Outcomes Through 5 Years in ASAP-TOO.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Oral anticoagulation (OAC) use in atrial fibrillation is suboptimal due to real or perceived bleeding risks. Left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is an alternative to OAC, but pivotal trials used OAC comparators.
OBJECTIVES: The study sought to assess the long-term safety and effectiveness of LAAC in patients deemed unsuitable for OAC.
METHODS: The ASAP-TOO trial was a multinational randomized trial of patients with atrial fibrillation, CHA2DS2-VASc (congestive heart failure, hypertension, age ≥75 years, diabetes mellitus, prior stroke or transient ischemic attack or thromboembolism, vascular disease, age 65-74 years, sex category) score ≥2, and OAC unsuitability; target enrollment was 888 patients. Patients were assigned 2:1 to LAAC with a Watchman device or control treatment-single antiplatelet therapy or no therapy. Device patients received dual antiplatelet therapy for 3 months and aspirin through 12 months. The primary effectiveness endpoint was ischemic stroke or systemic embolism; the primary safety endpoint was death, ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, or 7-day device/procedure-related events requiring major intervention.
RESULTS: Enrollment stopped early because of slow accrual, accentuated by the COVID-19 pandemic: only 481 patients were randomized (320 LAAC, 161 control treatment) and withdrawal was significant (7.8% LAAC, 24.2% control treatment), with disparate follow-up durations (median 876 days and 440.1 total patient-years of follow-up for control patients; median 1,768 days and 1,154.6 total patient-years of follow-up for LAAC patients), reducing statistical power. Patients were 75 ± 8 years of age, the CHA2DS2-VASc score was 4.6 ± 1.7, and 34% had prior intracranial/subdural hemorrhage. Implantation success was 97.8%. Only 31 of the 101 planned primary effectiveness events occurred, fewer than the 34 events required to trigger the first planned interim analysis. The primary safety endpoint occurred in 1.0% of implant-attempted patients, meeting the prespecified performance goal (P < 0.0001); there were 3 pericardial effusions requiring intervention. At up to 5 years, ischemic stroke or systemic embolism occurred in 7.8% with LAAC and 11.4% with control treatment (HR: 0.73; 95% CI: 0.35-1.52; P = 0.39). Major bleeding was 22.1% with LAAC and 15.7% with control treatment (HR: 1.64; 95% CI: 0.96-2.81; P = 0.067), concentrated during the first 3 months. In an exploratory analysis, disabling/fatal stroke was nominally less frequent with LAAC (2.2% vs 5.7%; HR: 0.32; 95% CI: 0.10-1.05).
CONCLUSIONS: In this prematurely terminated and underpowered trial, LAAC implantation was successful, with acceptable safety. Long-term estimates with LAAC were numerically favorable for thromboembolism but imprecise, while early bleeding was increased with the mandated antiplatelet regimen. These findings should be interpreted as exploratory and integrated with contemporary evidence and shared decision making. (Assessment of the WATCHMAN Device in Patients Unsuitable for Oral Anticoagulation [ASAP-TOO]; NCT02928497).

candidates.title: Left Atrial Appendage Closure in Atrial Fibrillation Patients With High Risk of Stroke and Bleeding: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is increasingly used as an alternative to oral anticoagulation for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation. Its comparative effectiveness and safety in patients at a high risk of both stroke and bleeding remain uncertain.
OBJECTIVES: We evaluated the efficacy and safety of LAAC vs contemporary medical therapy in a high-risk population using individual participant data from randomized trials.
METHODS: Bibliographic databases and trial registries through August 5, 2026, were searched for randomized trials comparing percutaneous LAAC with contemporary medical therapy in populations with a trial-level mean CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥4. A 1-stage common-effect analysis used Cox models stratified by trial and adjusted for age, sex, CHA2DS2-VASc score, and HAS-BLED score. Both primary outcomes were time to first stroke, systemic embolism, or cardiovascular/unknown death (efficacy) and time to first major bleeding (safety). A flexible time-varying Cox model was used for major bleeding. The protocol was submitted to PROSPERO (CRD420261335972).
RESULTS: CLOSURE-AF (Left Atrial Appendage CLOSURE in Patients With Atrial Fibrillation Compared to Medical Therapy) and PRAGUE-17 (Left Atrial Appendage Closure vs. Novel Anticoagulation Agents in Atrial Fibrillation) contributed 1,290 participants (647 assigned to LAAC and 643 to control). Median age was 77.3 years (Q1-Q3: 71.4-81.9 years), and 809 participants (62.7%) were men. The primary efficacy outcome occurred in 142 LAAC participants (21.9%) and 133 control subjects (20.7%) (adjusted HR: 0.98; 95% CI: 0.77-1.24; P = 0.842). Major bleeding occurred in 86 LAAC participants (13.3%) and 80 control subjects (12.4%) (adjusted HR: 1.03; 95% CI: 0.75-1.39; P = 0.874). The treatment effect on major bleeding varied over time (P for treatment-by-time interaction < 0.001), with a cumulative major bleeding incidence of 9.4% with LAAC vs 6.0% with control (absolute risk difference, 3.4 percentage points; 95% CI: 0.4-6.3 percentage points) at 1 year and 13.2% vs 12.1% (absolute risk difference, 1.1 percentage points; 95% CI: -2.8 to 5.0 percentage points) at 3 years.
CONCLUSIONS: In high-risk patients with atrial fibrillation, no statistically significant difference was detected between LAAC and contemporary medical therapy for the primary efficacy outcome or major bleeding. The major bleeding hazard varied over time, with higher early and lower later conditional hazard estimates; however, a cumulative bleeding benefit was not demonstrated by 3 years. Long-term randomized data are needed to improve the precision of later treatment-effect estimates.

candidates.title: Left Atrial Appendage Closure or Anticoagulation for Atrial Fibrillation: Navigating Heterogeneity in Clinical Evidence: JACC Evidence Review.
candidates.abstract: Left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has emerged as an alternative to long-term anticoagulation for preventing stroke or systemic embolism in selected patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) based on several randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that collectively enrolled >7,000 participants. In this JACC Evidence Review, we interpret the major RCTs as distinct experiments, clarify what each can and cannot establish, and offer a phenotype-based framework for interpreting the evidence. The most recent RCTs, OPTION, CLOSURE-AF, and CHAMPION-AF, have prompted efforts to pool the evidence into a single summary estimate. However, these trials are not one coherent evidence base; they are distinct clinical experiments that asked different questions. They differ in patient phenotype, comparator, device generation, postprocedure antithrombotic regimen, endpoint construction, and follow-up duration. Study-level meta-analysis of published reports remains methodologically valid for estimating the broad direction of effect of a device class, but when the component trials differ materially in patient phenotype, comparator, and outcome construction, the pooled estimate does not map to a common patient group or treatment decision. Patient eligibility as well as thromboembolic and bleeding risk varied markedly across trials. In addition, device technology has progressed, and comparators have evolved from warfarin to direct oral anticoagulants. Heterogeneity and insufficient details also exist about the antithrombotic therapy regimen in LAAC arms and adjunct antiplatelet therapy in control arms. Methodological issues further complicate interpretation, including the use of bleeding events (ie, the putative ancillary benefit of LAAC compared with anticoagulation) within composite endpoints tested for noninferiority, varying noninferiority margins, analytical approaches that may undermine the interpretation of noninferiority, and exclusion of periprocedural bleeding from primary safety endpoints in some trials. Finally, the standard of care for anticoagulation in AF has evolved, obviating concomitant aspirin use in stable individuals on therapeutic anticoagulation, thereby reducing bleeding risk compared with that of the control arm of LAAC RCTs. For most anticoagulation-eligible patients, anticoagulation remains the preferred first-line strategy. LAAC is a reasonable option when long-term anticoagulation is unsafe or unsustainable provided that procedural risk, adjunct antithrombotic feasibility, surveillance needs, and competing mortality are carefully considered. RCT evidence in this latter population is limited, and RCTs in other populations have features that limit their support for LAAC as an alternative to anticoagulation. Because LAAC and anticoagulation offer different types of risk, aligning the most applicable evidence with patient values through shared decision-making is central to care.

candidates.title: Comparison of Outcomes Between Men and Women Treated With Left Atrial Appendage Closure or Oral Anticoagulation After Catheter Ablation for Atrial Fibrillation: An OPTION Subanalysis.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Women sex is an established, nonmodifiable risk factor for adverse outcomes in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). Left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has been proposed as an alternative to oral anticoagulation (OAC) for stroke prevention in patients with AF; however, there are limited data on sex-based outcomes of LAAC following catheter ablation.
OBJECTIVES: This study sought to compare outcomes of LAAC vs OAC after AF ablation in men and women.
METHODS: Patients with AF and CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 in men and ≥3 in women were randomized 1:1 to either ablation + LAAC or ablation + OAC. The primary safety endpoint was nonprocedural major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding at 36 months. The primary efficacy endpoint was a composite of all-cause death, stroke, or systemic embolism at 36 months.
RESULTS: The study included 1,053 men and 546 women. LAAC and OAC demonstrated comparable primary efficacy events in men (HR: 0.96; 95% CI: 0.56-1.65; P = 0.88) and women (HR: 0.81; 95% CI: 0.41-1.62; P = 0.55), with no treatment-by-sex interaction (P interaction = 0.71). Procedural complication rates were similar at 2.3% in men and 3.7% in women with only 1 pericardial effusion in each group, not related to the index LAAC procedure. At 36 months, the primary safety endpoint was significantly lower in the device group among men (HR: 0.34; 95% CI: 0.23-0.50; P < 0.0001). In women, a similar but nonsignificant trend was observed (HR: 0.68; 95% CI: 0.42-1.09; P = 0.11), with a significant treatment-by-sex interaction (P interaction = 0.02). No significant difference was seen in the secondary safety endpoint across both treatment arms for either sex.
CONCLUSIONS: In this prespecified analysis of the OPTION (Comparison of Anticoagulation With Left Atrial Appendage Closure After AF Ablation [OPTION]) trial, stroke, systemic embolism, and mortality outcomes were not significantly different between LAAC and OAC following AF ablation in either men or women. Compared with OAC, LAAC demonstrated a greater magnitude of major and clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding reduction in men as compared with women. (Comparison of Anticoagulation With Left Atrial Appendage Closure After AF Ablation [OPTION]; NCT03795298).

candidates.title: Antithrombotic Therapy Management After Left Atrial Appendage Closure: Current Regimens, Evolving Evidence, and the Control Group Dilemma.
candidates.abstract: Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure is increasingly used for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation, particularly when long-term oral anticoagulation (OAC) is unsuitable. Although postprocedural antithrombotic therapy is necessary to prevent device-related thrombosis (DRT), it may increase bleeding and attenuate the benefit of avoiding long-term OAC. Uncertainty over the optimal antithrombotic strategy persists, with available randomized trials being small and heterogeneous. Direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) monotherapy and dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) are 2 common early strategies. In ANDES, DRT was numerically less frequent with DOAC than with DAPT (1.5% vs 4.1%). In ADALA, low-dose apixaban was associated with greater net benefit than DAPT (HR: 0.19; P = 0.02), although enrollment was prematurely stopped. A meta-analysis of randomized trials found significantly lower DRT with DOAC than with DAPT (risk ratio: 0.17). Current guidelines endorse regimens largely based on device-specific trial protocols or low-certainty evidence. During the initial postimplantation period, antithrombotic therapy should primarily aim to support device healing and prevent DRT, with treatment intensity tailored according to risk profile, concomitant indications, patient preferences, and the feasibility of imaging follow-up. Reassessment at 45 to 90 days should guide de-escalation once adequate device healing has been confirmed, with no fixed treatment stop date. In the absence of device-related complications, long-term OAC or DAPT should be continued only for concomitant indications, whereas continuation of single antiplatelet therapy or complete withdrawal of antithrombotic therapy should be individualized according to thrombotic and bleeding risk. Finally, definite or probable DRT generally warrants OAC, when feasible; in contrast, treatment decisions should not be based solely on the presence or size of a peridevice leak. This review critically appraises the available evidence and guideline recommendations and discusses how treatment intensity and duration may be tailored over time according to evolving thrombotic and bleeding risks.

candidates.title: Temporal Changes in Lipoprotein(a) Following Acute Coronary Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
candidates.abstract:
AIMS: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined cardiovascular risk factor generally considered stable over an individual's lifetime. Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) may transiently alter Lp(a) concentrations, complicating interpretation. We systematically evaluated temporal changes in Lp(a) following ACS.
METHODS: This PRISMA 2020-guided systematic review searched MEDLINE and Embase from database inception to February 2026. Eligible studies reported serial Lp(a) measurements at two or more time points after index ACS event. Exploratory random-effects meta-analysis of percent change in mean Lp(a) was performed.
RESULTS: Of 3,811 records, 16 studies comprising 1,396 patients met inclusion criteria. Lp(a) demonstrated a dynamic post-ACS trajectory. Using initial post-ACS measurements as the reference, pooled percent change in mean Lp(a) was non-significant at 24 hours post-ACS (+2.5%, 95% CI -6.8 to 11.7; p=0.602). Lp(a) was significantly higher at 7-14 days (+44.0%, 95% CI 4.0-84.1; p=0.031), 1 month (+28.3%, 95% CI 2.7-54.0; p=0.030), and 3-6 months (+22.2%, 95% CI 2.4-42.0; p=0.028). Across two studies, absolute Lp(a) increases >25 nmol/L occurred in 17% and 22% of patients by 3 and 6 months, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS: Lp(a) is not static post-ACS. Early post-ACS measurements may underestimate long-term concentrations and risk. Repeat measurement weeks to months later is most informative when initial post-ACS Lp(a) values are near clinical decision thresholds or would influence eligibility for emerging Lp(a)-lowering therapies.

candidates.title: Effect of discontinuing antihypertensives on perioperative hypotension in older patients before non-cardiac surgery: multicentre, randomised, double blind, controlled trial.
candidates.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether discontinuing versus continuing angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) on the morning of surgery reduces perioperative hypotension in older patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery.
DESIGN: Multicentre, randomised, double blind, placebo controlled trial.
SETTING: Five tertiary teaching hospitals in China, November 2020 to December 2023.
PARTICIPANTS: 2036 older patients (60-80 years) using ACE inhibitors or ARBs for at least two weeks and scheduled for non-cardiac surgery under general anaesthesia.
INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomised to receive their usual ACE inhibitor or ARB or a placebo in identical capsules on the morning of surgery.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: The primary outcome was the incidence of perioperative hypotension (mean blood pressure <65 mm Hg or a ≥30% decrease from baseline requiring treatment). Secondary outcomes included duration of hypotension, requirement for a vasopressor, intraoperative fluid volume, postoperative hypotension, and 30 day complications (neurocognitive disorders, major cardiocerebral events) or mortality.
RESULTS: 2012 patients (mean age 68.8 years; 54.4% male) completed the study: 1004 were included in the antihypertensive group and 1008 in the no antihypertensive group. The incidence of perioperative hypotension was lower in the no antihypertensive group (314/1008, 31.2%) versus antihypertensive group (457/1004, 45.5%): adjusted odds ratio 0.52 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.43 to 0.63); absolute risk difference -14.4% (95% CI -18.5% to -10.1%); P<0.001. The duration of hypotension and requirement for a vasopressor were both reduced in the no antihypertensive group: adjusted mean difference -1.3 minutes (95% CI -1.8 to -0.8 minutes) and 28.5% v 41.1%; adjusted odds ratio 0.54 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.66). Intraoperative fluid volume, postoperative hypotension, 30 day complications, and mortality did not differ significantly between groups.
CONCLUSIONS: Discontinuing ACE inhibitors or ARBs on the morning of surgery in older patients with hypertension statistically significantly reduced perioperative hypotension and the requirement for vasopressors without increasing 30 day complications or mortality. This simple strategy provides high certainty evidence for preoperative drug management in this patient population.

candidates.title: Beyond Coronary Artery Disease: Etiologies and Outcomes of the Shark-Fin ECG Pattern: A Systematic Review.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The shark-fin sign (SFS) is a rare, high-risk electrocardiographic pattern reported in commonly linked with obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD).
OBJECTIVE: To characterize the electrocardiographic patterns, etiologies, and clinical outcomes associated with the SFS.
METHODS: We systematically reviewed PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, and Cochrane from inception through May 20, 2026, including all studies with participant-level data.
RESULTS: Eighty-five papers involving 104 patients were included; 66.3% had non-obstructive etiologies. The obstructive CAD patients were predominantly male (97.1%), while other etiologies were predominantly female (60.8%). Among CAD cases, the left main coronary artery (LMCA)/proximal left anterior descending artery (LAD) was the culprit in 75.0%, and SFS localization matched coronary anatomy in 91.4%. VT/VF and death each occurred in 37.1%, with adverse outcomes confined to those with LMCA/LAD lesions. Among other etiologies, Takotsubo syndrome (TTS, 31.7%), vasospasm (14.4%), myocarditis (6.7 %) and neurologic emergencies (4.8%) were the most frequently reported. VT/VF occurred in 43.4% and 27.5% died. Among patients with TTS, 63.6% experienced VT/VF or death, compared with ventricular arrhythmias in 66% of patients with vasospasm.
CONCLUSION: SFS is a high-risk ECG pattern rather than a diagnosis and warrants urgent etiologic evaluation and cardiac monitoring. Most published data are derived from patients without established CAD. LMCA/LAD disease, TTS, and coronary vasospasm were associated with particularly high-risk hospitalizations. Primary non-cardiac causes should also be considered when clinically suspected.

candidates.title: Comparative Clinical and Procedural Outcomes Among Three Pulsed Field Ablation Systems for Atrial Fibrillation: A Prospective Real-World Study.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pulsed Field Ablation (PFA) is a non-thermal ablation technology for atrial fibrillation. Several PFA systems are available, with distinct catheter designs and energy delivery protocols. Direct comparisons between PFA systems remain limited.
OBJECTIVE: This study compared the procedural characteristics, safety, and efficacy of three contemporary PFA technologies in routine clinical practice.
METHODS: Consecutive patients undergoing their first pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) using the circular multielectrode array catheter (CMAC)(PulseSelectTM), the variable-loop circular catheter (VLCC)(VaripulseTM) or the lattice-tip catheter (LTC)(AfferaTM) were prospectively included. Freedom from any atrial arrhythmia (AA) was evaluated using 12-lead electrocardiography and 24-hour Holter at 3, 6 and 12 months, followed by routine clinical follow-up.
RESULTS: A total of 198 patients (CMAC:91, VLCC:50, LTC: 57) were included. Acute PVI was achieved in all patients (median age, 68 [61.0, 76.0] years; 127 male (64.1%); 97 paroxysmal (49.0%)). The procedure and ablation times were longest in the LTC group. During a mean follow-up of 352.4±207.2 days, the estimated 12-month freedom from AA recurrence beyond the 8-week blanking period was comparable among the CMAC, VLCC, and LTC groups (76.9%, 71.6%, and 78.8%; log-rank p=0.72). In adjusted multivariable Cox regression, PFA system choice was not associated with AA recurrence (LTC vs. CMAC: HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.39-1.52, p=0.45; VLCC vs. CMAC: HR 1.16, 95% CI 0.58-2.34, p=0.67). One major complication (0.51%, ischemic stroke (CMAC)) occurred.
CONCLUSION: In this prospective real-world study, PVI with the CMAC, VLCC, and LTC showed comparable efficacy and safety outcomes, while procedural profiles differed.

candidates.title: Anticoagulation in Subclinical Atrial Fibrillation: An Evidence-Based Framework for Individualized Management.
candidates.abstract: The increasing use of wearable monitoring technologies and cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) has led to frequent incidental detection of subclinical atrial fibrillation (SCAF), yet the role of long-term anticoagulation remains uncertain. Growing evidence indicates that SCAF is a separate clinical entity on the continuous spectrum of atrial disease and not just a precursor to clinical disease. We propose that anticoagulation in SCAF should be guided by integrating arrythmia burden, baseline clinical risk and the degree of structural atrial cardiomyopathy in addition to life expectancy and patient preferences. This review synthesizes data from observational studies, randomized clinical trials, and post-hoc analyses to provide a comprehensive and practical framework for individualized anticoagulation, and risk-benefit considerations.

candidates.title: Pulsed Field or Cryoballoon Pulmonary Vein Isolation for Atrial Fibrillation in Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Atrial fibrillation (AF) and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) frequently coexist, worsening prognosis. While catheter ablation confers clinical benefits in this high-risk population, comparative data between novel non-thermal pulsed field ablation (PFA) and established cryoballoon ablation (CBA) for AF-therapy in patients with HFrEF are limited.
OBJECTIVE: To compare the efficacy and safety of PFA- with CBA-based pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) in patients with AF and HFrEF (left ventricular ejection fraction ≤40%).
METHODS: This retrospective, international multicenter study included patients with HFrEF undergoing first-time PVI-only procedures between 2018 and 2025. Propensity-score matching (1:1 ratio) was applied to balance baseline characteristics. The primary efficacy endpoint was the first recurrence of any atrial tachyarrhythmia after a 3-month blanking period. Secondary measures included safety events and procedural efficiency.
RESULTS: A total of 700 patients from 12 German and Canadian centers were included, with 420 patients analyzed following propensity-score matching. At 12 months, freedom from atrial tachyarrhythmia recurrence with PFA was comparable to CBA (Kaplan-Meier estimates, 65.0% vs. 67.8%; hazard ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.77 to 1.55; P=0.61). No statistically significant differences in observed safety outcomes were detected. PFA significantly improved procedural efficiency with shorter total procedure duration (58±22min vs. 72±22min; P<0.001), left-atrial dwell time (42±16min vs. 52±17min; P<0.001) and lower contrast dye use (0 ml [IQR 0-15] vs. 47 ml [IQR 30-56], P<0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: In patients with AF and HFrEF, PFA-based PVI achieves similar rhythm-control efficacy and safety compared with CBA, while significantly enhancing procedural efficiency.

candidates.title: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism after Total Hip or Knee Replacement.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Studies comparing aspirin with anticoagulants for venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis after total hip or knee arthroplasty have had conflicting results.
METHODS: In a comparative-effectiveness noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned patients undergoing elective hip or knee arthroplasty to receive aspirin (81 mg twice daily), warfarin (to a target international normalized ratio of 2.0), or rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) for 30 days. The composite primary effectiveness outcome (death from any cause or symptomatic VTE) and primary safety outcome (bleeding, reoperation for wound problems, or myocardial infarction) were evaluated through 6 months in a blinded fashion. The noninferiority margin for the risk difference was 0.69 percentage points.
RESULTS: Among 18,883 participants who had undergone randomization, 15,317 (7214 with hip arthroplasty and 8103 with knee arthroplasty) were included in the primary per-protocol analysis. A primary effectiveness outcome event occurred in 77 of 6090 participants (1.26%) in the aspirin group, in 52 of 4231 (1.23%) in the warfarin group, and in 47 of 4996 (0.94%) in the rivaroxaban group; a primary safety outcome event occurred in 177 (2.91%), 142 (3.36%), and 174 (3.48%), respectively. In pairwise comparisons, 6-month risks of a primary effectiveness outcome event were 1.24% and 0.94% for aspirin versus rivaroxaban (difference, 0.30 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.20 to 0.81); 1.24% and 1.01% for aspirin versus warfarin (difference, 0.23 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.34 to 0.81); and 1.13% and 1.10% for warfarin versus rivaroxaban (difference, 0.03 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.57 to 0.63). Risks of a primary safety outcome event were 3.70% and 3.02% for rivaroxaban versus aspirin (difference, 0.68 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.04 to 1.41); 3.65% and 2.88% for warfarin versus aspirin (difference, 0.77 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.04 to 1.58); and 3.59% and 3.61% for rivaroxaban versus warfarin (difference, -0.02 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.89 to 0.85). Intention-to-treat analyses yielded similar results.
CONCLUSIONS: Aspirin prophylaxis after total hip or knee arthroplasty was not noninferior to rivaroxaban or warfarin with respect to death or symptomatic VTE. Warfarin and rivaroxaban were not noninferior to aspirin for safety. (Funded by the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute; PEPPER ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT02810704.).

candidates.title: First and Subsequent Major Cardiovascular Events With Oral Semaglutide in High-Risk Type 2 Diabetes: A Secondary Analysis of the SOUL Randomized Clinical Trial.
candidates.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: In the Semaglutide Cardiovascular Outcomes Trial (SOUL), oral semaglutide reduced the risk of a first 3-point major adverse cardiovascular event (3-P MACE; including nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, and cardiovascular [CV] death). Total event analyses, assessing both first and subsequent events, can contribute to a better understanding of the impact of interventions on the total burden of disease; however, the effects of oral semaglutide on subsequent events are unknown.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effect of oral semaglutide vs placebo on total 3-P MACE.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This was a prespecified secondary analysis of the double-blind, placebo-controlled, event-driven, phase 3b SOUL randomized clinical trial, conducted from June 2019 to September 2024 with a median (IQR) follow-up of 49.5 (44.0-54.9) months at 444 centers in 33 countries. Participants had type 2 diabetes and atherosclerotic CV disease and/or chronic kidney disease. Data were analyzed from December 2024 to August 2025.
INTERVENTIONS: Once-daily oral semaglutide (maximal dose 14 mg) or placebo, in addition standard of care.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Occurrence of total (first and subsequent) 3-P MACE.
RESULTS: Overall, 9650 participants (median [IQR] age, 66.0 [61.0-72.0] years; 6860 [71.1%] male) were randomized 1:1. In the oral semaglutide group, fewer first and subsequent 3-P MACE occurred (683 total; 579 first and 104 subsequent events) compared with placebo (791 total; 668 first and 123 subsequent events) (mean ratio, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.76-0.97; P = .01). For the end point of 3-P MACE plus non-CV death, there were 138 fewer total events with oral semaglutide (910 events) compared with placebo (1048 events) (mean ratio, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.79-0.95; P = .004). As previously reported, adverse events led to treatment discontinuation in 749 (15.5%) and 559 (11.6%) participants receiving oral semaglutide and placebo, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS: Oral semaglutide reduced the risk of first plus subsequent 3-P MACE vs placebo, highlighting the benefit of oral semaglutide in reducing the total burden of clinical morbidity and mortality in this high-risk population.
